rationale:
The example `requirements.sdk.graph.hierarchical-paths` is a concrete case. The input is `ReviewNodeId::Requirement(vec!["a","b","c"])`. The expected output is the path `["requirement","a","b","c"]`. It cites `requirements.sdk.graph.node_path_method`, which requires `node_path` to be deterministic (1:1 and stable).

`ReviewNodeId` appears only in the book chapter `md/requirements/sdk/graph.md` as an illustrative domain. The test therefore has no real `ReviewNodeId` or `Domain` implementation to exercise.

The test `hierarchical_requirement_identity_maps_each_component_to_a_path_segment` in `crates/trust-but-verify/tests/contracts.rs` builds the same shape. It defines a local enum with a `Requirement(Vec<String>)` variant and a `node_path` closure that prefixes "requirement". The closure builds a real `NodePath` with `NodePath::new`. The test feeds it the identity `["a","b","c"]` and has two assertions:
- `segments()` equals `["requirement","a","b","c"]`. This checks the expected mapping.
- Calling `node_path` twice on the same identity gives equal results. This checks the determinism that `node_path_method` requires.

The identity and the expected segments both come from the example's text. The test uses the name `HabeasNodeId` instead of `ReviewNodeId`. That is a cosmetic difference, because the enum is illustrative and not part of the code. Every outcome the example states is checked.
